Validating arguments and results

Source: vignettes/validation.Rmd
validation.Rmd
library(fnware)

Checking inputs is the same few lines at the top of every function: test the type, test the range, build an error message. validate_args() moves those checks out of the body and into a decorator, and validate_return() does the same for the value a function hands back.

scale_by := validate_args(x = is.numeric, n = ~ .x > 0) %@% function(x, n = 1) {
  x * n
}
scale_by(2, 3)
## [1] 6
scale_by("a", -1)
## Error:
## ! Invalid arguments.
## ✖ `x`: failed validation.
## ✖ `n`: failed validation.

Both problems are reported in one error, so the caller fixes everything in one pass instead of one failure at a time.

What counts as a validator

A validator is any function that takes the value. fnware does not know about any particular checking package, so base predicates, your own functions and packages like checkmate all go in the same way. A validator passes only when it returns exactly TRUE. Anything else fails:

It returns Result
TRUE passes
a string fails, and the string is the message
FALSE or anything else fails with a generic message
(it signals an error) the error propagates unchanged

A formula is turned into a function with rlang::as_function(), so ~ .x > 0 is shorthand for \(.x) .x > 0.

Messages

Returning a string is the convention used by checkmate’s check_*() functions, and it is easy to follow in your own code:

check_string <- function(x) {
  if (is.character(x) && length(x) == 1L) TRUE else "must be a single string"
}

greet := validate_args(name = check_string) %@% function(name) {
  paste("Hello", name)
}
greet("Ada")
## [1] "Hello Ada"
greet(1)
## Error:
## ! Invalid arguments.
## ✖ `name`: must be a single string

With checkmate installed, validate_args(x = checkmate::check_numeric) works the same way, and so does a validator that throws, such as checkmate::assert_numeric. A thrown error is not collected with the others: it stops validation and reaches the caller as it is.

Which arguments are checked

validate_args() checks the value each named argument has when the function runs, so defaults are validated too. A default that breaks its own rule is caught on the first call:

bad_default := validate_args(n = ~ .x > 0) %@% function(x, n = -1) x * n
bad_default(2)
## Error:
## ! Invalid arguments.
## ✖ `n`: failed validation.

Arguments you do not name are never touched, so an unvalidated argument can still be missing or lazy. A validated argument is forced when the call starts rather than when the body first uses it.

Names are checked against the function’s arguments when it is decorated, so a typo fails straight away rather than silently validating nothing:

validate_args(z = is.numeric) %@% function(x) x
## Error in `validate_args()`:
## ! `validate_args()` names not in the function's arguments: `z`.

Validating the result

validate_return() takes one validator for the returned value. It is a post-condition: it catches a function that returns the wrong thing, which is a bug in the function rather than in the caller.

parse_port := validate_return(~ is.integer(.x) && .x > 0) %@% function(s) {
  as.integer(s)
}
parse_port("8080")
## [1] 8080
parse_port("-1")
## Error:
## ! Invalid return value.
## ✖ failed validation.

Visibility is preserved, so an invisible() result stays invisible.

Handling failures

Failures have class fnware_validation_error, so callers can handle them apart from other errors:

tryCatch(
  scale_by("a"),
  fnware_validation_error = function(e) "bad input"
)
## [1] "bad input"

Combining with other decorators

Decorators stack, and order matters. Validation usually goes outermost so bad input is rejected before any work is done:

lookup := validate_args(id = is.numeric) %@%
  cache %@%
  function(id) {
    cat("  looking up", id, "\n")
    id * 2
  }
lookup(1)
##   looking up 1
## [1] 2
lookup(1)
## [1] 2

Putting it outside retry() matters for the same reason: a validation error is the caller’s mistake, and retrying it only repeats the mistake.
